*Essential data revealing why startups fail and how founders can make better early decisions*


The startup landscape presents a sobering reality for ambitious entrepreneurs. According to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics,[77.7% of establishments](https://www.bls.gov/bdm/us_age_naics_00_table7.txt) founded in the year ending March 2024 survived their first year. That measure differs from the widely cited[90% startup failure estimate](https://www.failory.com/blog/startup-failure-rate) , which has no single universally agreed definition or timeframe. Understanding these differences helps founders prioritize market validation, manage funding carefully, and build products that address real customer needs. For those looking to test their ideas without extensive development overhead,[Floot](https://floot.com/en) offers a full-stack app-building platform that connects with compatible AI assistants through an MCP connector, providing managed infrastructure to build and test working applications.


## **Key Takeaways**


- **Market validation matters.** In an analysis of 101 failed startups, lack of market need appeared in[42% of cases](https://s3-us-west-2.amazonaws.com/cbi-content/research-reports/The-20-Reasons-Startups-Fail.pdf) . Start with a[working MVP](https://floot.com/blog/ai-app-builders-mvp-development) before expanding development spending.
- **Survival depends on the cohort.** BLS data shows that[52.3% of establishments](https://www.bls.gov/bdm/us_age_naics_00_table7.txt) founded in March 2021 survived four years.[Floot's managed infrastructure](https://floot.com/docs/integrations/whats-built-in) can reduce setup work, not eliminate business risk.
- **Funding alone is insufficient.** Failed startups reported cash shortages alongside market and team problems. Compare[building costs](https://floot.com/en/pricing) with the ongoing costs of hosting and validation.
- **Experience can help.** One founder-statistics compilation reports success rates of[18% among first-timers](https://ff.co/startup-statistics-guide/) and[30% among repeat founders](https://ff.co/startup-statistics-guide/) . Explore[non-technical founder guidance](https://floot.com/blog/non-technical-founder-statistics) when planning an initial product.
- **AI development can reduce friction.** Floot connects supported AI assistants with app infrastructure, subject to connector permissions. Its[connector guide](https://floot.com/docs/integrations/build-from-claude-and-chatgpt) explains how the workflow differs from buying separate AI building credits.


## **Understanding the Startup Failure Rate: What the Numbers Tell Us**


Startup outcomes vary by business model, funding source, and how researchers define success. A venture seeking rapid growth is not identical to a small employer establishment. Understanding these baseline differences helps founders set realistic expectations and identify where to focus their efforts.


### **1. 90% of startups are commonly estimated to fail overall**


The commonly cited[90% failure rate](https://www.failory.com/blog/startup-failure-rate) is a broad estimate for innovative startups, not a universal failure rate for all newly established businesses. Actual survival rates depend on how startups are defined, the cohort studied, and the period measured. Failory also notes that many early startup projects never register a formal business. Treat the figure as an illustration of risk rather than an individualized prediction.


### **2. First-time founders have a reported 18% success rate**


New entrepreneurs face a steep climb, with one Founders Forum compilation reporting just[18% success](https://ff.co/startup-statistics-guide/) on an initial venture. This gap between first-timers and experienced founders highlights the possible value of entrepreneurial learning. However, the figure is not a universal probability for every business type, and success depends on the study's definition. Founders should evaluate demand and capabilities, not rely on a single average.


### **3. Previously failed founders have a reported 20% success rate**


Founders who have experienced failure are reported to succeed on[20% of subsequent ventures](https://ff.co/startup-statistics-guide/) in the same compilation. The reported two-percentage-point gap from first-time founders suggests that lessons from failure can be valuable. It does not prove that failure itself causes improvement. Identifying mistakes in hiring, positioning, and spending can make those lessons practical when testing a new business idea.


### **4. Previously successful founders have a reported 30% success rate**


Those who have succeeded before enjoy a reported[30% success rate](https://ff.co/startup-statistics-guide/) with their next venture. The reported 12-percentage-point difference from first-timers illustrates an association between past outcomes and subsequent performance. Prior success may bring networks, experience, and credibility, but it does not guarantee another successful company. A new venture still needs an identifiable customer, sensible economics, and evidence of demand.


## **Why Startups Fail: Common Pitfalls for First-Time Founders**


Identifying the specific causes of failure allows founders to address weaknesses proactively. Several figures below come from[CB Insights' analysis](https://s3-us-west-2.amazonaws.com/cbi-content/research-reports/The-20-Reasons-Startups-Fail.pdf) of 101 failed startup post-mortems. These percentages describe reasons mentioned in that historical sample, can overlap, and are not universal startup failure rates. Other figures use separate compilations and should not be added together.


### **5. 42% of failed startups cited no market need**


Building something nobody wants was cited in[42% of the 101](https://s3-us-west-2.amazonaws.com/cbi-content/research-reports/The-20-Reasons-Startups-Fail.pdf) failed startup post-mortems examined by CB Insights. This was the most frequently mentioned reason in that historical sample. Founders can avoid assuming their solution is wanted by testing specific customer problems before committing major resources. Early interviews and a functional MVP offer better evidence than enthusiasm for an untested feature list.


### **6. A separate compilation attributes 34% of failures to weak product demand**


A separate startup-statistics compilation attributes[34% of failures](https://www.demandsage.com/startup-statistics/) to insufficient product demand. This overlaps conceptually with the previous market-need figure and should not be added to it. The source provides a different breakdown without a directly comparable study population. The practical lesson remains that founders should identify a reachable audience, confirm purchasing interest, and distinguish polite feedback from actual willingness to pay.


### **7. 29% of failed startups cited running out of cash**


Cash depletion appeared in[29% of cases](https://s3-us-west-2.amazonaws.com/cbi-content/research-reports/The-20-Reasons-Startups-Fail.pdf) among the failed startup post-mortems in the CB Insights research. Running out of money is often linked with deeper problems, including slow traction, high costs, or difficulty raising additional funds. Capital efficiency helps founders preserve time to test hypotheses. Tracking runway, recurring expenses, and customer demand together is more useful than treating fundraising as the only solution.


### **8. A separate compilation attributes 16% of failures to financial problems**


One separate breakdown attributes[16% of startup failures](https://www.demandsage.com/startup-statistics/) to financial problems. This is not the same dataset as the 29% cash-depletion figure and cannot be combined with it. Financial problems can include poor pricing, inadequate margins, or operational inefficiency. Founders should regularly review actual cash flow, not just revenue, and test whether customer payments can cover the costs of serving them.


### **9. 23% of failed startups cited the wrong team**


Team problems, including conflicts, missing skills, and poor hiring decisions, appeared in[23% of cases](https://ff.co/startup-statistics-guide/) in the CB Insights sample, a figure also summarized by Founders Forum. Finding the right people for the right roles is rarely straightforward. Founding team mismatches often become clearer as workloads and decisions grow more demanding. Defining responsibilities and resolving disagreements early can help prevent avoidable operational friction.


### **10. A separate compilation attributes 22% of failures to marketing problems**


A separate compilation attributes[22% of startup failures](https://www.demandsage.com/startup-statistics/) to marketing problems, rather than the 14% reported in the older CB Insights sample. Marketing missteps demonstrate that building a functional product is only part of the challenge. Customer acquisition channels, messaging, positioning, and go-to-market strategy must align with how target customers discover and purchase solutions. These figures describe different sources and should not be combined.


### **11. 19% of failed startups cited being outcompeted**


Competition was mentioned in[19% of cases](https://ff.co/startup-statistics-guide/) in the failed startup post-mortems analyzed by CB Insights. Competitive pressure can come from direct rivals, established alternatives, or customers who prefer their existing workflows. Founders must articulate why customers should switch and whether the proposed improvement is compelling enough. Comparing actual customer behavior against assumptions helps reveal weaknesses before marketing and development costs expand.


### **12. 18% of failed startups cited pricing or cost problems**


Pricing or cost problems appeared in[18% of cases](https://ff.co/startup-statistics-guide/) in the CB Insights analysis. Pricing too low can leave insufficient margin for continued investment, while pricing too high may limit demand. A sustainable model needs to account for acquisition expenses, infrastructure, support, and delivery costs. Testing prices with real customers provides stronger evidence than making assumptions from competitor price lists alone.


### **13. 17% of failed startups cited a poor product**


A poor or user-unfriendly product was cited in[17% of cases](https://ff.co/startup-statistics-guide/) among the failed startup post-mortems. Even when customers want a solution, confusing workflows or unreliable features can prevent repeat usage. Technical debt accumulated during rapid development may also undermine product quality. Founders should test essential tasks with actual users, resolve failures, and prioritize improvements that support the problem the product is meant to solve.


### **14. 14% of failed startups cited ignoring customers**


In the CB Insights analysis, ignoring customers was identified in[14% of cases](https://ff.co/startup-statistics-guide/) . This measures a reason mentioned among failed companies, not the probability that any company ignoring feedback will close. Building in isolation makes it harder to spot incorrect assumptions. Regular feedback sessions, observed behavior, and thoughtful prioritization help founders distinguish useful product signals from isolated requests.


## **How Many Businesses Fail in the First 5 Years? A Deeper Dive**


The timeline of business establishment survival shows a substantial decline during the first year, followed by additional closures over subsequent years. These BLS data concern U.S. private-sector establishments, not only high-growth startups. Comparing cohorts requires attention to both their opening dates and their follow-up periods.


### **15. 77.7% of the 2024 U.S. establishment cohort survived one year**


According to Bureau of Labor Statistics data,[77.7% of establishments](https://www.bls.gov/bdm/us_age_naics_00_table7.txt) founded in the year ending March 2024 survived through March 2025. This measures employer establishments rather than startups exclusively. It also means 22.3% closed within the first year. Founders should treat early operations as a serious test of demand, expense control, and the ability to deliver consistently to customers.


### **16. 52.3% of the 2021 U.S. establishment cohort survived four years**


For the cohort established in the year ending March 2021,[52.3% of establishments](https://www.bls.gov/bdm/us_age_naics_00_table7.txt) remained active in March 2025 according to BLS data. This illustrates the survival challenge during the first several years of business. The figure is cumulative, not a fourth-year-only survival rate. Continued operations require sufficient revenue, responsive decisions, and an ability to adjust as customer needs and costs evolve.


### **17. 65.8% of the 2023 U.S. establishment cohort survived two years**


Bureau of Labor Statistics data shows that[65.8% of establishments](https://www.bls.gov/bdm/us_age_naics_00_table7.txt) founded in the year ending March 2023 remained active through March 2025. This cumulative two-year survival measure is lower than the same cohort's first-year rate. Founders should use such figures for context rather than as predictions about individual startups. Actual results depend on industry, financial resources, and the strength of the business model.


### **18. 51.3% of the 2020 U.S. establishment cohort survived five years**


At the five-year mark,[51.3% of establishments](https://www.bls.gov/bdm/us_age_naics_00_table7.txt) founded in the year ending March 2020 were still operating in March 2025, according to BLS data. This threshold reflects sustained operation, not necessarily profitability or rapid growth. Surviving businesses may have successfully navigated changes in demand, costs, and competition. Founders should distinguish remaining open from meeting their financial and strategic objectives.


### **19. 34.6% of the 2015 U.S. establishment cohort survived ten years**


BLS data reports that[34.6% of establishments](https://www.bls.gov/bdm/us_age_naics_00_table7.txt) founded in the year ending March 2015 remained active in March 2025. This implies a cumulative closure rate of 65.4% over ten years. The calculation covers employer establishments, not a startup-only sample. Long-term sustainability calls for adapting to customer expectations, changing market conditions, and recurring operating costs beyond the initial launch phase.


### **20. 32.6% of the 2014 U.S. establishment cohort survived eleven years**


Long-term survival remains challenging, with[32.6% of establishments](https://www.bls.gov/bdm/us_age_naics_00_table7.txt) founded in the year ending March 2014 still operating in March 2025 according to BLS data. This is an eleven-year cumulative survival rate, rather than a measure of business profitability. The figure illustrates how openings decline across a long horizon. Businesses may close for numerous reasons, including voluntary exits, ownership changes, or financial difficulties.


## **Small Business Failure Rate: Distinctions and Drivers**


Small businesses face challenges that differ from venture-backed startup projects, although many patterns overlap. Capital constraints influence strategic choices, with bootstrapped ventures often prioritizing revenue and profitability earlier. The following figures come from published compilations of business financing estimates rather than a single comparable startup cohort.


### **21. 77% of businesses reportedly use personal savings for initial funding**


A startup-statistics compilation reports that[77% of businesses](https://www.demandsage.com/startup-statistics/) rely on founders' personal savings for initial funding. The estimate should not be mistaken for a current census of all startup financing sources. Personal funding can preserve ownership, but it also increases the founder's direct financial exposure. Testing demand before committing substantial savings and documenting startup costs can help inform safer early decisions.


### **22. About 58% of small business owners launched with under $25,000**


A compilation reports that almost[58% of owners](https://www.demandsage.com/startup-statistics/) launched their ventures with less than $25,000 in initial capital. Limited funding often requires founders to prioritize essential functions and test their offerings before expanding. However, startup costs differ greatly across industries and locations. Software founders should budget not only for building but also for hosting, compliance, support, and customer acquisition.


### **23. 31% of employer firm startups reportedly began with under $10,000**


For startups planning to employ staff, a published compilation reports that[31% of these startups](https://www.demandsage.com/startup-statistics/) began with less than $10,000 in startup capital. This figure concerns an employer-firm category rather than all new businesses. Starting with limited resources may require early revenue and careful hiring decisions. Founders should model how long their available funds can cover payroll, infrastructure, sales efforts, and unexpected expenses.

## **What Percentage of Small Businesses Fail in the First Year? Early-Stage Insights**


The first year presents distinct challenges around market entry, initial traction, and operational fundamentals. Getting the basics right matters more than growth optimization while founders validate assumptions and establish foundational systems. Regional figures below are historical observations, not current regional rankings.


### **24. 78.2% of the 2023 U.S. establishment cohort survived one year**


Bureau of Labor Statistics data shows that[78.2% of establishments](https://www.bls.gov/bdm/us_age_naics_00_table7.txt) founded in the year ending March 2023 survived through March 2024. That leaves 21.8% that closed during the first year. The result differs slightly from the March 2024 cohort, demonstrating why a single survival figure cannot represent every period. Early customer feedback, reliable operations, and cash management remain important during launch.


### **25. The Pacific division recorded 84.6% first-year survival for the 2021 cohort**


Geographic factors can influence business survival. BLS historical data reports[84.6% first-year survival](https://www.bls.gov/opub/ted/2024/1-year-survival-rates-for-new-business-establishments-by-year-and-location.htm) in the Pacific division for businesses born in 2021, the highest one-year observation in its historical series through 2022. It is not a current year ranking. Differences across regions can reflect economic conditions, industry concentrations, local costs, and customer markets, so comparisons require matching periods.


### **26. The South Atlantic division recorded 71.4% first-year survival for the 2008 cohort**


The BLS historical series records[71.4% first-year survival](https://www.bls.gov/opub/ted/2024/1-year-survival-rates-for-new-business-establishments-by-year-and-location.htm) in the South Atlantic division among businesses born in 2008, its lowest regional observation through 2022. This is not evidence that the division currently has the nation's lowest survival rate. Regional outcomes depend on the economic period as well as local business conditions. Founders should seek recent, industry-specific data before choosing a location.


## **Startup Grind: The Founder's Journey and Resilience**


The human element of entrepreneurship can influence outcomes. Research on age, experience, teams, and adaptation challenges common assumptions about who can build successful companies. These results come from distinct studies and should not be read as guarantees about any individual founder.


### **27. The average founder in a major U.S. study was 42 years old**


Contrary to the young-founder stereotype, MIT researchers reported an[average age of 42](https://mitsloan.mit.edu/ideas-made-to-matter/20-year-old-entrepreneur-a-lie) among U.S. entrepreneurs who started businesses that hired at least one employee. The study drew on administrative data rather than a survey of aspiring founders. Experience may provide domain knowledge, networks, and relevant professional skills. The average does not imply that founders younger or older than 42 cannot succeed.


### **28. Founders of the highest-growth startups averaged 45 years old**


In the same U.S. research, founders of the highest-growth startups had an[average age of 45](https://mitsloan.mit.edu/ideas-made-to-matter/20-year-old-entrepreneur-a-lie) . The finding challenges the assumption that high-growth companies are typically started by people in their twenties. It does not mean that age alone creates successful outcomes. Industry experience, access to resources, and the ability to identify valuable problems may be more useful areas for founders to examine.


### **29. A 60-year-old founder was 3 times as likely to succeed as a 30-year-old in one study**


Research summarized by MIT reports that a 60-year-old founder was[3 times as likely](https://orbit-kb.mit.edu/hc/en-us/articles/206072746-Am-I-too-old-to-start-a-company/) as a 30-year-old founder to start a successful company under the study's measures. This is an observed association, not a guarantee based on age. Differences in professional experience, networks, and resources may be relevant. Founders of any age should evaluate their own capabilities and market evidence.


### **30. Balanced founding teams raised 30% more funding and saw 2.9x user growth**


An early Startup Genome report found that teams with one technical and one business founder raised[30% more money](https://www.dentonsventurebeyond.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/10/StartupGenomeReport1_Why_Startups_Succeed_v2.pdf) and recorded[2.9x user growth](https://www.dentonsventurebeyond.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/10/StartupGenomeReport1_Why_Startups_Succeed_v2.pdf) compared with technical-heavy or business-heavy teams. The findings show an association, not proof that adding a co-founder automatically improves results. Complementary expertise may help with both product delivery and customer acquisition when responsibilities are clearly defined.


### **31. Startups that pivoted once or twice recorded 3.6x better user growth**


The Startup Genome report found that companies pivoting one or two times had[3.6x user growth](https://www.dentonsventurebeyond.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/10/StartupGenomeReport1_Why_Startups_Succeed_v2.pdf) and raised 2.5 times as much money as those pivoting more often or not at all. This historical association does not prove that pivoting causes growth. Founders benefit from recognizing when evidence challenges their assumptions while avoiding repeated changes that prevent a product from developing a clear direction.


## **Strategic Approaches to Startup Funding: Beyond the Initial Boost**


Understanding funding dynamics helps founders make informed decisions about capital strategy. The relationship between funding and success is more complex than simply raising more money, and large funding rounds are not typical for every new business.


### **32. An estimated 0.05% of startups receive VC funding**


A widely repeated estimate suggests that only[0.05% of startups](https://www.failory.com/blog/startup-failure-rate) secure venture capital financing. Failory attributes the figure to an older funding-source summary, but the denominator and measurement period are not clearly specified. It should be treated as a rough illustration of selectivity, not an exact current probability. Most small business founders consider savings, revenue, loans, or other financing approaches instead.


### **33. Global venture funding reached $427.1 billion in 2025**


The OECD reports[approximately $427.1 billion](https://www.oecd.org/en/publications/venture-capital-investments-in-artificial-intelligence-through-2025_a13752f5-en/full-report.html) in worldwide venture capital investment during 2025, based on its analysis of Preqin data. Funding totals depend on the source's definitions and coverage, so published estimates from other trackers may differ. The distribution of capital across industries was uneven. Founders should not interpret an aggregate global funding figure as money necessarily available to their own sector or stage.


### **34. AI firms attracted $258.7 billion in venture funding in 2025**


According to the same OECD analysis, AI firms secured[$258.7 billion in global](https://www.oecd.org/en/publications/venture-capital-investments-in-artificial-intelligence-through-2025_a13752f5-en/full-report.html) venture investment in 2025, equivalent to about 61% of the report's overall total. The share reflects the OECD's classification and dataset, not every possible venture funding tracker. This concentration demonstrates how uneven sector funding can be. Founders outside AI should evaluate investor fit rather than assume market-wide totals reflect their opportunities.


### **35. 75% of venture-backed companies did not return cash in one study**


Harvard Business School lecturer Shikhar Ghosh's research, summarized by Failory, found that[75% of companies](https://www.failory.com/blog/startup-failure-rate) in a historical sample did not return cash to investors. That investor-return definition is different from closing or going bankrupt. Venture capital outcomes follow an uneven distribution in which relatively few companies produce large returns. Founders should distinguish investor expectations from their own measures of business success.


### **36. Only 40% of small businesses were reported as profitable in one compilation**


One Zippia compilation reports that[40% of small businesses](https://www.zippia.com/advice/small-business-revenue-profit-margin/) are profitable at a given time, while approximately 30% break even and another 30% operate at a loss. Its figure should be treated as a compiled estimate rather than a universal current census. Profitability requires revenue to exceed costs, including staff, operations, and tools. A working product alone does not establish a sustainable business model.

## **Frequently Asked Questions**


### **What is the average startup failure rate?**


A commonly cited estimate suggests that 90% of startups eventually fail, but its definition and timeframe are not standardized. In BLS data, the March 2024 private-sector establishment cohort had[77.7% survival](https://www.bls.gov/bdm/us_age_naics_00_table7.txt) , while the March 2015 cohort had[34.6% survival](https://www.bls.gov/bdm/us_age_naics_00_table7.txt) . These establishment figures should not be confused with the broader startup estimate. Read the[MVP validation guide](https://floot.com/blog/ai-app-builders-mvp-development) to plan practical early tests.


### **What are the top three reasons startups fail?**


In CB Insights' analysis of 101 failed startups, the three most frequently mentioned reasons were[no market need (42%)](https://s3-us-west-2.amazonaws.com/cbi-content/research-reports/The-20-Reasons-Startups-Fail.pdf) ,[cash shortages (29%)](https://s3-us-west-2.amazonaws.com/cbi-content/research-reports/The-20-Reasons-Startups-Fail.pdf) , and[the wrong team (23%)](https://ff.co/startup-statistics-guide/) . The same study allows multiple reasons per company, so these percentages cannot be added. Market validation, capital management, and team composition deserve attention, although these historical findings cannot predict an individual company's outcome.


### **How can non-technical founders reduce startup risk?**


Non-technical founders can test demand before significant spending, build a functional MVP rather than relying on mockups, track customer feedback, and maintain cash reserves. Floot can reduce backend setup work through its managed app infrastructure, but founders remain responsible for assessing quality and business viability. The[non-technical founder guide](https://floot.com/blog/non-technical-founder-statistics) provides further context on getting a product to its first users.


### **Can founders build a scalable app without extensive coding knowledge?**


Yes, platforms such as Floot help founders develop applications through supported AI assistants. Floot supplies managed Postgres, authentication, storage, and hosting, while the connected assistant handles development within its permissions. This reduces manual setup but does not guarantee performance, security, or unlimited capacity. Founders should test realistic workloads, review reliability limits, and understand hosting costs before wider deployment.


### **What role does funding play in startup success?**


Funding can provide time for validation, product development, and customer acquisition, but it does not guarantee success. In a historical analysis,[29% of failed startups](https://s3-us-west-2.amazonaws.com/cbi-content/research-reports/The-20-Reasons-Startups-Fail.pdf) cited running out of cash, while a separate investor-return study found that[75% of companies](https://www.failory.com/blog/startup-failure-rate) did not return cash to investors. These measures are different. Review[Floot pricing](https://floot.com/en/pricing) alongside all other operating costs when budgeting for an initial application.
